questions.q: What is a "shot" in the context of running a quantum circuit?
options: A single gate operation within a circuit
One full, independent execution of the entire circuit from initialization through measurement
A unit of simulated time
The number of qubits in the circuit
questions.explain: Each shot is a complete independent run: prepare the qubits, apply every gate, measure, record the outcome, then discard the state and start over for the next shot.

questions.q: For a true probability p=0.5, what is the standard error formula for the observed frequency over N shots?
options: SE = p / N
SE = sqrt(p(1-p)/N)
SE = N / p
SE = p(1-p) * N
questions.explain: This is standard binomial sampling theory: the standard error of an observed frequency is sqrt(p(1-p)/N), the same math behind polling margins of error.

questions.q: At N=100 shots with true p=0.5, a real seeded draw gave `{'0': 47, '1': 53}`. Given a standard error of about 0.05 at this N, is this result consistent with the true 50/50 probability?
options: No, it proves the simulator is biased
Yes, an observed 53% is well within the roughly ±9.8 percentage point band expected at N=100
No, because it should have come out exactly 50/50
It cannot be evaluated without running more shots first
questions.explain: With SE ≈ 0.05 at N=100, deviations of several percentage points from the true value are completely expected, not evidence of any problem.

questions.q: Going from N=1024 (SE ≈ 0.0156) to N=8192 (SE ≈ 0.0055) shots is an 8x increase in shot count. What is the resulting scaling factor on the standard error?
options: Exactly 8x smaller
Exactly 2x smaller
Roughly sqrt(8) ≈ 2.8x smaller, consistent with 1/sqrt(N) scaling
No change at all
questions.explain: Standard error scales as 1/sqrt(N), so an 8x increase in shots only reduces the standard error by roughly sqrt(8) ≈ 2.8x, not the full 8x.

questions.q: Why isn't it always best practice to simply maximize the number of shots used in an experiment?
options: Qiskit caps shots at a hard maximum of 1024
More shots always make results less accurate
Because of 1/sqrt(N) scaling, each additional shot buys diminishing statistical benefit, while every shot costs real time and, on real hardware, queue time or money
Shots have no effect on statistical uncertainty at all
questions.explain: Since halving standard error requires 4x the shots, returns diminish quickly. Meanwhile every shot has a real cost (time, queue credits, money on cloud hardware), making shot count a genuine engineering tradeoff.
